chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Statistical Toolkit for Spotting Reversion

lessons.title: Autocorrelation and the Half-Life of Mean Reversion

children.text: Chapter 1 gave you the AR(1) equation with a coefficient called phi controlling how strongly a deviation gets pulled back toward its mean. It left phi as an abstract dial. This lesson turns it into two numbers you can actually use. The first, autocorrelation, is a diagnostic: it tells you whether a series behaves like a mean-reverting process at all. The second, half-life, is the practical answer every reversion trader actually wants: given a deviation right now, how many trading days should you expect to wait for half of it to correct?

body.text: Negative autocorrelation in a price's deviation from its mean is the statistical fingerprint of mean reversion: an above-average day tends to be followed by a below-average one. Once you estimate how strong that pull is, the half-life formula converts it into the single most practical number for a reversion trader, the expected number of trading days for a deviation to shrink by half.

children.text: Autocorrelation: Does Yesterday's Move Predict Today's?

markDefs.definition: The correlation between a time series and a lagged version of itself, for example today's value against yesterday's value.

children.text: the correlation of a series with a lagged version of itself

. Applied to raw price levels, lag-1 autocorrelation is almost always close to 1, since today's price is nearly always close to yesterday's price, which tells you nothing useful and is really just restating that prices don't teleport overnight. The autocorrelation that actually matters here is the autocorrelation of the deviation from a rolling mean, the same quantity the z-score in Lesson 5 was built to measure. If a stock closing above its 20-day average today makes it statistically more likely to close below that average tomorrow, the deviation series has negative autocorrelation, and that is the fingerprint of mean reversion. If closing above average today makes another above-average close more likely tomorrow, the deviation has positive autocorrelation, and that is the fingerprint of momentum, exactly the opposing thesis from Lesson 2.

body.caption: The lag-k autocorrelation of the deviation series X_t (price minus its rolling mean). rho_1 is the lag-1 autocorrelation most commonly used in practice.

columns.label: Negative autocorrelation
points: An above-average day tends to be followed by a below-average one
The statistical fingerprint of mean reversion
Deviations decay back toward zero over time
This is the case this course is built to trade

columns.label: Positive autocorrelation
points: An above-average day tends to be followed by another above-average one
Deviations tend to persist or grow rather than shrink
This is the opposing thesis covered conceptually in Lesson 2

children.text: Here is the useful mathematical fact that connects this lesson back to Chapter 1's AR(1) equation. For a well-behaved AR(1) process, the lag-1 autocorrelation of the deviation series is exactly phi. This means you do not need any exotic statistics to estimate phi. You can regress today's deviation on yesterday's deviation, a single straight-line fit, and the slope of that regression is your estimate of phi. A slope close to 0 means the series snaps back almost immediately. A slope close to 1 means it barely reverts at all within a normal trading horizon and starts to look more like a random walk.
Half-Life: How Long Until a Deviation Shrinks by Half

Once you have phi, a deviation of size D today is expected to shrink to D times phi after one day, D times phi squared after two days, and D times phi to the power n after n days, decaying geometrically toward zero. Setting phi to the power n equal to one-half and solving for n gives you the half-life, the number of trading days it takes, on average, for a deviation to shrink to half its starting size.

body.caption: Since 0 < phi < 1, ln(phi) is negative, which makes the half-life a positive number of trading days.

cells: Very fast reversion, likely dominated by noise and hard to capture after costs
Fast reversion, a candidate for a short-holding-period strategy
A practical, tradeable speed for a swing-style reversion strategy
Slow reversion, requires patience and a wider stop
Barely distinguishable from a random walk over normal trading horizons

body.title: A deviation of 100 decaying with phi = 0.85 (half-life ≈ 4.3 days)

body.text: Half-life is what turns a statistical property into a trading decision. It sets your expected holding period, and by extension a sensible time-based exit: if a trade built on a 4-day half-life still has not moved after three weeks, the statistical basis for holding it has likely expired, whatever the price is doing. Chapter 7 uses half-life directly to size holding periods and time-based exits. As a rule of thumb, a half-life under about a week is genuinely tradeable, and a half-life stretching into months is a warning sign that the series is closer to a random walk than to a reliable mean reverter.

children.text: Estimating Phi and Half-Life in Python

body.code:
import numpy as np

# 'deviation' is a pandas Series: price minus its rolling mean
x = deviation.shift(1).dropna()
y = deviation.loc[x.index]

# Slope of y regressed on x is the lag-1 autocorrelation estimate, phi
phi = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)[0]

half_life = -np.log(2) / np.log(phi)

print(f"phi = {phi:.3f}, half-life = {half_life:.1f} trading days")
body.caption: Estimating phi by regressing today's deviation on yesterday's, then converting it to a half-life in trading days.

body.title: Compute the half-life
body.prompt: A regression of a stock's deviation series on its own one-day lag gives an estimated phi of 0.80. What is the half-life, in trading days, rounded to one decimal place?
body.explanation: Half-life = -ln(2) / ln(0.80) = -0.6931 / -0.2231 = 3.11, which rounds to 3.1 trading days. A phi of 0.80 implies a fairly quick reversion, roughly half the deviation should correct within about three trading days.

body.title: Faster or slower reversion?
body.question: Stock A has an estimated phi of 0.60. Stock B has an estimated phi of 0.97. Which stock has the shorter half-life, and therefore faster mean reversion?
options: Stock A, because a lower phi means deviations decay faster each day
Stock B, because a higher phi means deviations decay faster each day
Both stocks have identical half-lives regardless of phi
Half-life cannot be determined from phi alone
body.explanation: A lower phi means a smaller fraction of the deviation survives each day, so it shrinks to half its size faster. Stock A's phi of 0.60 gives a half-life of about 1.4 trading days, while Stock B's phi of 0.97 gives a half-life of about 22.8 trading days. Lower phi always means faster reversion.

cards.definition: The correlation between a time series and a lagged version of itself. Applied to a price's deviation from its mean, negative autocorrelation signals mean reversion and positive autocorrelation signals momentum.
The coefficient in an AR(1) process controlling how much of a deviation survives from one period to the next. Equal to the lag-1 autocorrelation of the deviation series.
The expected number of trading days for a deviation from the mean to shrink to half its original size, calculated as minus the natural log of 2 divided by the natural log of phi.

points: Autocorrelation of a price's deviation from its mean, not of the raw price itself, is what reveals mean reversion. Negative autocorrelation is the signature of reversion, positive autocorrelation is the signature of momentum.
For an AR(1) process, the lag-1 autocorrelation of the deviation series equals phi, so a simple regression of today's deviation on yesterday's gives you a direct estimate of phi.

Half-life, calculated as minus ln(2) divided by ln(phi), converts phi into the single most practical number for a reversion trader: the expected number of trading days for a deviation to shrink by half.
A short half-life (days) suggests a genuinely tradeable reversion. A half-life stretching into months suggests the series is closer to a random walk than to a reliable mean reverter.
Chapter 7 uses half-life directly to set expected holding periods and time-based exits for a mean reversion strategy.
